title: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation v. Nawab Khan Gulab Khan
summary: Twenty-nine families had built huts on the footpaths of a main road in Ahmedabad. When the Municipal Corporation moved to clear the encroachment in 1982, the Gujarat High Court stopped it, ruling that they could not be removed until they were given suitable accommodation and a hearing. The Corporation appealed to the Supreme Court. The Court accepted that the right to shelter is part of the right to life and pressed the Corporation to frame a scheme for the families, but held that nobody can claim a right to occupy a public road and that a full hearing is not required before clearing a street encroachment. It allowed the appeal and modified the High Court's order: those of the original families who met the income conditions were to be offered a site or a flat under the Corporation's housing schemes, and anyone who did not take up the offer could be evicted after 21 days' notice. The Corporation largely won, but the eligible families left with an offer of housing. This is the reference point for a grievance about a municipal body demolishing or evicting occupants of public land without notice or a fair hearing.
excerpts: a modicum of reasonable notice for removal, say two weeks or 10 days, and personal service on the encroachers or substituted service by fixing notice on the property is necessary.
It would, therefore, be the duty of the State to provide right to shelter to the poor and indigent weaker sections of the society in fulfillment of the Constitutional objectives.

Holding — the Court held that a municipal corporation's power to remove encroachments on public land must be exercised through a just, fair and reasonable procedure that includes reasonable prior notice, informed by the right to shelter under Article 21.
bench: K. Ramaswamy, J. and others

outcome.winner: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, subject to housing the eligible families
outcome.verdict: The Corporation's appeal was allowed: eligible original dwellers were to be offered sites or tenements under its schemes, and others could be removed on 21 days' notice.

parties.petitioner: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (appealing)
parties.respondent: Nawab Khan Gulab Khan and other pavement dwellers

title: Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association of India
summary: Section 30 of the Punjab Excise Act, 1914, as it applied in Delhi, made it an offence to employ any woman, or any man under 25, in any premises where liquor is served to the public — shutting women out of jobs in bars, hotels and restaurants. The Hotel Association of India challenged the provision and the Delhi High Court struck it down so far as it concerned women. A group of Delhi citizens appealed to the Supreme Court to have the ban restored, arguing the State was entitled to protect women from the risks of such work. The Court dismissed their appeal: a law that excludes women from an occupation for their own supposed good is discrimination unless the State can strictly justify it, and the answer to an unsafe workplace is to make it safe, not to bar women from it. It also struck down the bar on employing men under 25. The Hotel Association won, and women could be employed where liquor is served. This is the reference point for a grievance about a law or workplace rule that excludes women from employment on paternalistic grounds.
excerpts: It is to be borne in mind that legislations with pronounced "protective discrimination" aims, such as this one, potentially serve as double edged swords. Strict scrutiny test should be employed while assessing the implications of this variety of legislations.
restriction keeping in view a citizen's right to be considered for employment, which is a facet of the right to livelihood do not stand judicial scrutiny.

Holding — the Court struck down the statutory bar on women's employment in premises serving liquor, holding that such paternalistic restrictions fail strict scrutiny and violate the guarantees of equality, non-discrimination and the right to livelihood under Articles 14, 15 and 19.
bench: S.B. Sinha and Harjit Singh Bedi, JJ.

outcome.winner: The Hotel Association of India, and women seeking such work
outcome.verdict: The appeal was dismissed and the ban on employing women, and on employing men under 25, in liquor-serving premises was struck down.

parties.petitioner: Anuj Garg and other citizens seeking to restore the ban (appealing)
parties.respondent: Hotel Association of India

title: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India
summary: An organisation working against bonded labour wrote a letter to the Supreme Court about workers in stone quarries in Faridabad, near Delhi, who were held in bondage and lived without clean water, medical care or protective equipment. The Court treated the letter itself as a writ petition, sent commissioners to investigate conditions in the quarries, and rejected the objection that it could not proceed this way. It held that the right to life means the right to live with human dignity, including humane conditions of work, and that once a worker is shown to be doing forced labour the court will presume he is a bonded labourer unless the employer proves otherwise. It issued detailed directions to identify, release and rehabilitate the workers under the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 and to enforce their other labour-law rights. The workers won. This is the reference point for grievances about bonded labour, unpaid or underpaid work, child labour and unsafe working conditions.
excerpts: Holding — the Court held that whenever it is shown that a labourer is made to provide forced labour, the court will raise a presumption that he is required to do so in consideration of an advance or other economic consideration received by him, and is therefore a bonded labourer.

Holding — the Court held that the right to live with human dignity enshrined in Article 21 derives its life breath from the Directive Principles of State Policy, and includes protection of the health and strength of workers and just and humane conditions of work.

Holding — the Court held that a letter addressed to it disclosing a violation of the fundamental rights of a disadvantaged group can be treated as a writ petition under Article 32, and appointed commissioners to investigate the working conditions in the quarries.
bench: Bhagwati J. and others

outcome.winner: The quarry workers
outcome.verdict: The petition was allowed, with a presumption of bonded labour in the workers' favour and detailed directions to release and rehabilitate them.

parties.petitioner: Bandhua Mukti Morcha, an anti-bonded-labour organisation
parties.respondent: Union of India, the State of Haryana and the quarry contractors

statutes.name: Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979

title: Consumer Education and Research Centre v. Union of India
summary: Workers in asbestos factories were breathing in asbestos dust and developing asbestosis and other incurable lung diseases, often without protective equipment, monitoring of the air they breathed, or regular medical checks. The Consumer Education and Research Centre went to the Supreme Court on their behalf. The Court held that the right to health and to medical care while in service is part of a worker's right to life under Article 21, and that an employer running a hazardous industry carries that obligation. It directed factories to keep long-term health records for every worker, to use a more sensitive test for detecting asbestos disease, to provide compulsory health insurance, and to have workers re-examined by the National Institute of Occupational Health, with compensation of one lakh rupees payable to every worker found to be suffering from asbestosis. The workers won. This is the reference point for a grievance about a workplace exposing employees to hazardous substances without safety measures or health monitoring.
excerpts: The right to health to a worker is an integral facet of meaningful right to life to have not only a meaningful existence but also robust health and vigour without which worker would lead life of misery.

it must be held that the right to health and medical care is a fundamental right under Article 21 read with Articles 39(c), 41 and 43 of the Constitution and make the life of the workman meaningful and purposeful with dignity of person.

Holding — the Court directed employers in hazardous industries such as asbestos manufacturing to maintain health records, provide compulsory health insurance and periodic medical examinations, holding that a worker's right to health and medical care is part of Article 21.
bench: K. Ramaswamy, A.M. Ahmadi and M.M. Punchhi, JJ.

outcome.winner: The asbestos factory workers
outcome.verdict: The petitions were allowed, with directions on health records, medical examination and insurance, and one lakh rupees compensation for each worker found to have asbestosis.

parties.petitioner: Consumer Education and Research Centre, for asbestos workers
parties.respondent: Union of India, the State Governments and the asbestos industry

title: Chameli Singh v. State of U.P.
summary: The Uttar Pradesh Government compulsorily acquired farmland in Bijnor district to build houses for Dalit families, and invoked the urgency power in the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 to take possession without the usual hearing of objections. Chameli Singh and the other landowners challenged the acquisition, arguing that there was no real urgency and that taking their land destroyed their livelihood, contrary to Article 21. The Supreme Court rejected both arguments and upheld the acquisition, holding that providing housing to the poor is a public purpose urgent enough to justify the shortened procedure, and that acquisition following the law, with compensation and solatium, is not a deprivation of the right to livelihood. In the course of the judgment it held that the right to shelter is itself a fundamental right, and means far more than a roof: adequate space, a safe structure, clean surroundings, water, electricity and sanitation. The landowners lost, and the housing scheme for Dalit families went ahead. This is the reference point for a grievance about being denied adequate, livable housing rather than bare shelter.
excerpts: shelter, therefore, includes adequate living space, safe and decent structure, clean and decent surroundings, sufficient light, pure air and water, electricity, sanitation and other civic amenities like roads etc. so as to have easy access to his daily avocation.
The right to shelter, therefore, does not mean a mere right to a roof over one's head but right to all the infrastructure necessary to enable them to live and develop as a human being.

Holding — the Court held that the right to shelter is a fundamental right under Articles 19(1)(e) and 21 of the Constitution, encompassing adequate living space, a safe structure, clean surroundings, sanitation and other basic civic amenities, and not merely a roof over one's head.
bench: K. Ramaswamy and B.N. Kirpal, JJ.

outcome.winner: The State of Uttar Pradesh and the families to be housed
outcome.verdict: The appeals were dismissed and the land acquisition for housing the poor was upheld, while the right to shelter was held to mean decent, serviced accommodation.

parties.petitioner: Chameli Singh and other landowners (appealing)
parties.respondent: State of Uttar Pradesh

title: Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2G Spectrum)
summary: In 2008 the Department of Telecommunications handed 122 telecom licences and 2G spectrum to selected companies at prices fixed back in 2001, using a first-come-first-served method whose cut-off date was moved at short notice. The Centre for Public Interest Litigation and others challenged the giveaway in the Supreme Court. The Court held that natural resources such as spectrum are held by the State as a trustee for the people, and that handing them out by an arbitrary method, rather than an open auction, violated the guarantee of equality. It cancelled all 122 licences, ordered spectrum to be allotted afresh by auction, and imposed costs on the companies that had benefited. The petitioners won. This is the reference point for grievances about arbitrary allocation of public resources, favouritism in government contracts and regulatory capture.
excerpts: The State is the legal owner of the natural resources as a trustee of the people and although it is empowered to distribute the same, the process of distribution must be guided by the constitutional principles including the doctrine of equality and larger public good.

Holding — the Court held that the exercise undertaken by the officers of the Department of Telecommunications between September 2007 and March 2008 was wholly arbitrary, capricious and contrary to public interest, apart from being violative of the doctrine of equality.
Holding — the Court quashed the licences granted to the private respondents and directed that spectrum be reallocated by auction.
bench: G.S. Singhvi and A.K. Ganguly JJ.

outcome.winner: Centre for Public Interest Litigation
outcome.verdict: All 122 licences were quashed, spectrum was ordered to be reallocated by auction, and costs were imposed on the benefiting companies.

parties.petitioner: Centre for Public Interest Litigation and other petitioners
parties.respondent: Union of India (Department of Telecommunications) and the licensee companies

statutes.name: Telecom Regulatory Authority of India Act, 1997

title: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India
summary: Chemical factories at Bichhri village in Udaipur district, Rajasthan, produced H-acid and dumped untreated waste and toxic sludge on the open ground. The poison seeped into the earth and the groundwater, ruining the wells the villagers drank from and the soil they farmed, and the damage outlasted the factories, which were shut down in 1989. The Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action, an environmental group, brought the villagers' case to the Supreme Court. The Court held the companies absolutely liable for the harm and applied the polluter-pays principle: whoever causes the pollution must bear the whole cost of undoing it. It directed the Central Government to work out what the clean-up would cost and recover that amount from the companies under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, and ordered the companies to pay the petitioner's costs. The villagers and the petitioner won. This is the reference point for a grievance about industrial effluent contaminating groundwater or soil relied on by a nearby community.
excerpts: This writ petition filed by an environmentalist organization brings to light the woes of people living in the vicinity of chemical industrial plants in India.
Setting up such highly polluting industry in a critical ground water area was essentially ill-conceived.

Holding — the Court held the polluting industries absolutely liable to bear the cost of remediating the contaminated groundwater and soil at Bichhri village and of compensating the affected villagers, applying the polluter-pays principle.
bench: B.P. Jeevan Reddy and B.N. Kirpal, JJ.

outcome.winner: The villagers of Bichhri
outcome.verdict: The polluting companies were held absolutely liable, and the Central Government was directed to assess the remediation cost and recover it from them.

parties.petitioner: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action, for the villagers of Bichhri
parties.respondent: Union of India and the chemical companies operating at Bichhri

statutes.name: Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974

title: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
summary: Acting on the Mandal Commission's report, the Union Government reserved 27% of central government posts for Other Backward Classes in 1990, and the next year added a further 10% for poorer people not covered by any existing reservation. Indra Sawhney and others challenged both, arguing that they destroyed equality of opportunity. Nine judges of the Supreme Court upheld the 27% reservation for backward classes and held that caste may legitimately be used to identify a backward class, but required that the better-off “creamy layer” within those classes be excluded so that the benefit reaches those who need it. It struck down the extra 10% based purely on economic criteria, held that reservations should not ordinarily exceed half of the posts, and ruled that reservation does not extend to promotions. The challengers largely lost: the backward-class reservation survived, but with limits the Court imposed. This is the reference point for a grievance about the validity or scope of caste-based reservation in public employment.
excerpts: Article 14 enjoins upon the state not to deny to any person "equality before the law" or "the equal protection of the laws" within the territory of India.
The doctrine of equality has many facets. It is a dynamic, and an evolving concept.

Holding — the Court held that reservation of posts for socially and educationally backward classes, subject to defined limits and exclusion of the 'creamy layer', is a permissible form of affirmative action consistent with the guarantee of equality under Article 14.
bench: M.H. Kania, M.N. Venkatachaliah, S. Ratnavel Pandian, T.K. Thommen and others (nine-judge bench)

outcome.winner: Mixed — mainly the Government, with court-imposed limits
outcome.verdict: The 27% reservation for backward classes was upheld subject to exclusion of the creamy layer and a 50% ceiling, while the 10% economic reservation was struck down.

parties.petitioner: Indra Sawhney and others challenging the reservation orders
parties.respondent: Union of India

title: Kharak Singh v. State of U.P.
summary: Kharak Singh had been charged with dacoity and released when no evidence was found against him, but the Uttar Pradesh police continued to treat him as a suspect under their surveillance regulations: they visited his house at night and woke him, kept watch over him, tracked his movements and maintained records on him. He challenged the regulations in the Supreme Court. The majority struck down the rule permitting night-time domiciliary visits, holding that a person's home and sleep are part of personal liberty under Article 21, but upheld the rest of the surveillance, taking the view that the Constitution contained no general right to privacy. Two judges dissented and would have struck the whole scheme down. The result was mixed: he stopped the night visits but remained under watch. The majority's view on privacy was overruled in 2017 by the nine-judge bench in Puttaswamy. This is the reference point for an early grievance about intrusive police surveillance of a person's home.
excerpts: these extracts would show that an unauthorised intrusion into a person's home and the disturbance caused to him thereby, is as it were the violation of a common law right of a man -an ultimate essential of ordered liberty, if not of the very concept of civilization.
"Domiciliary visits" is defined in the Oxford English Dictionary as "Visit to a private dwelling, by official persons, in order to search or inspect it."

Holding — the Court, by majority, struck down nightly domiciliary visits under the police surveillance regulation as violative of Article 21 for want of an authorising law, while upholding the other surveillance measures; Subba Rao J.'s dissent read a broader right to privacy into personal liberty under Article 21.
bench: N. Rajagopala Ayyangar, B.P. Sinha, Syed Jaffer Imam, K. Subba Rao and J.C. Shah, JJ.

outcome.winner: Mixed — the night visits were struck down, the rest of the surveillance was upheld
outcome.verdict: Domiciliary night visits were declared unconstitutional and stopped; the remaining surveillance regulations survived, over a celebrated dissent.

parties.petitioner: Kharak Singh
parties.respondent: State of Uttar Pradesh and its police

title: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak)
summary: Weeks after the Bhopal disaster, oleum gas escaped from a Shriram chemical plant in a crowded part of Delhi, harming workers and people living around it. The public-interest lawyer M.C. Mehta asked the Supreme Court to hold the company answerable. The Court laid down a new and stricter rule, absolute liability: an enterprise running a hazardous industry owes an absolute duty to the community, must compensate everyone harmed by an accident, and cannot rely on the usual excuses, with compensation scaled to the size of the company so that it actually deters. It directed the Delhi Legal Aid and Advice Board to file compensation claims on behalf of the victims. The victims won the rule that still governs industrial disasters in India. This is the reference point for a grievance about a hazardous industry injuring the community around it.
excerpts: We are of the view that an enterprise which is engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry which poses a potential threat to the health and safety of the persons working in the factory and residing in the surrounding areas owes an absolute and nondelegable duty to the community to ensure that no harm results to anyone on account of hazardous or inherently dangerous nature of the activity which it has undertaken.
The measure of compensation in such kind of cases must be co-related to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise because such compensation must have a deterrent effect.
Holding — the Court held that the power under Article 32 extends to forging new remedies and fashioning new strategies designed to enforce fundamental rights, including awarding compensation.
bench: Bhagwati C.J. and others

outcome.winner: M.C. Mehta and the gas-leak victims
outcome.verdict: Absolute liability was laid down for hazardous industry, and the Legal Aid Board was directed to bring the victims' compensation claims against the company.

parties.petitioner: M.C. Mehta, a public-interest lawyer
parties.respondent: Union of India and the Shriram chemical company

title: National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India
summary: Transgender people in India had no way to have their gender recognised in law, and were pushed to the margins of education, employment, healthcare and public life, often forced to identify as male or female against their sense of themselves. The National Legal Services Authority brought their case to the Supreme Court. The Court held that a person has the right to decide their own gender — male, female or third gender — and that insisting on surgery as the price of recognition is immoral and illegal, because the guarantees of equality, non-discrimination, free expression and dignity apply to transgender persons in full. It directed the Union and State Governments to grant legal recognition of the third gender, treat transgender persons as a socially and educationally backward class for reservations in education and public employment, and provide medical care, separate public toilets and welfare schemes. The petitioners won. This is the reference point for a grievance about denial of legal recognition or equal treatment on grounds of gender identity.
excerpts: Hijras, Eunuchs, apart from binary gender, be treated as "third gender" for the purpose of safeguarding their rights under Part III of our Constitution and the laws made by the Parliament and the State Legislature.

Transgender persons' right to decide their self-identified gender is also upheld and the Centre and State Governments are directed to grant legal recognition of their gender identity such as male, female or as third gender.

Holding — the Court held that transgender persons have the right to self-identify their gender as male, female or third gender, and that denial of this legal recognition violates the rights to equality, non-discrimination and dignity under Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21.
bench: K.S. Radhakrishnan and A.K. Sikri, JJ.

outcome.winner: Transgender persons
outcome.verdict: Self-identified gender was recognised in law, and governments were directed to provide recognition, reservations and welfare measures.

parties.petitioner: National Legal Services Authority and transgender petitioners
parties.respondent: Union of India and the State Governments

title: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
summary: Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, a colonial-era provision, punished “carnal intercourse against the order of nature” and was used to treat consenting adults in same-sex relationships as criminals, with the fear and blackmail that followed from it. The dancer Navtej Singh Johar and others petitioned the Supreme Court. Five judges held unanimously that Section 377, so far as it criminalises consensual sexual acts between adults in private, violates the rights to equality, to non-discrimination, to free expression and to a life of dignity and privacy, and they overruled the Court's own 2013 decision that had upheld the provision. Section 377 continues to apply to non-consensual acts, acts involving children, and bestiality. The petitioners won. This is the reference point for grievances about discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender or identity, and about being denied equal treatment or access.
excerpts: Holding — the Court held that Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, in so far as it criminalises consensual sexual conduct between adults in private, is violative of Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21 of the Constitution.
Constitutional morality cannot be martyred at the altar of social morality and it is only constitutional morality that can be allowed to permeate into the Rule of Law.
The choice of a partner, the desire for personal intimacy and the yearning to find love and fulfilment in human relationships have a universal appeal, straddling age and time.
bench: Five-judge Constitution Bench

outcome.winner: The petitioners and LGBT persons
outcome.verdict: Section 377 was struck down so far as it criminalised consensual adult conduct in private, and the contrary 2013 decision was overruled.

parties.petitioner: Navtej Singh Johar and other petitioners
parties.respondent: Union of India

statutes.name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012

title: Nestlé India Ltd. v. Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
summary: In 2015 India's food regulator banned Maggi noodles after laboratory tests reported lead above the permitted limit and objected to the packet's “No added MSG” claim. Nestlé India challenged the ban in the Bombay High Court. The Court set the ban orders aside, because Nestlé had never been given a hearing and the samples had not been tested in properly accredited laboratories as the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 requires. It ordered fresh testing in three accredited laboratories, and allowed the company to make and sell the noodles again only if the lead was found within permitted limits. Nestlé won on procedure, but still had to prove the product was safe before it could return to shelves. This is the reference point for a grievance about an unsafe or mislabelled food product and about a regulator acting without due process.
excerpts: Holding — the Bombay High Court set aside the orders of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India and the State Food and Drug Administration banning the product, holding that they were passed in breach of the principles of natural justice because no opportunity of hearing was given before the ban.

Holding — the Court directed that fresh samples be tested in three laboratories accredited by the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories, and that no coercive action be taken until those results were available.
Holding — the Court recorded that the statutory scheme of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 requires testing and appeal procedures to be followed before a product is withdrawn from the market.
bench: V. M. Kanade and B. P. Colabawalla, JJ.

outcome.winner: Nestlé India
outcome.verdict: The ban orders were set aside for lack of a hearing and proper testing, and fresh tests in three accredited laboratories were ordered before sale could resume.

parties.petitioner: Nestlé India Ltd.
parties.respondent: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India and the State food authorities

title: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
summary: The Bombay Municipal Corporation decided to evict pavement and slum dwellers in Bombay and demolish their huts, many of them people who had come to the city for work and lived beside the places they worked. The journalist Olga Tellis and the dwellers challenged the evictions in the Supreme Court, saying that losing their homes would destroy their livelihoods. The Court held that the right to life includes the right to livelihood, so an eviction that takes away a person's means of living must follow a procedure that is just and fair. But it also held that nobody has the right to occupy a footpath or other public space, so the Corporation could still clear them after due notice. The result was mixed: the dwellers established a principle that protects people across India to this day, but did not win the right to stay, and the Court ordered only that evictions wait until after the monsoon and that censused dwellers be offered alternative sites. This is the reference point for grievances about eviction, demolition, slum clearance and displacement.
excerpts: The sweep of the right to life conferred by Article 21 is wide and far reaching. It does not mean merely that life cannot be extinguished or taken away as, for example, by the imposition and execution of the death sentence, except according to procedure established by law. That is but one aspect of the right to life. An equally important facet of that right is the right to livelihood because, no person can live without the means of living, that is, the means of livelihood.

If the right to livelihood is not treated as a part of the constitutional right to live, the easiest way of depriving a person of his right to life would be to deprive him of his means of livelihood to the point of abrogation.

Holding — the Court held that the procedure for eviction must be just, fair and reasonable, and directed that the dwellers be given notice and, in stated cases, alternative accommodation before removal.
bench: Chandrachud C.J. and others

outcome.winner: Mixed — the principle went to the dwellers, the power to evict stayed with the Corporation
outcome.verdict: Eviction was held to require a just and fair procedure, but was allowed to proceed after the monsoon, with alternative sites for censused dwellers.

parties.petitioner: Olga Tellis, pavement dwellers and slum dwellers of Bombay
parties.respondent: Bombay Municipal Corporation and the State of Maharashtra

title: People's Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India
summary: Reports that the telephones of politicians had been tapped led the People's Union for Civil Liberties to challenge the Government's interception powers under the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, which named no procedure and carried no safeguards against misuse. The Supreme Court held that a telephone conversation in a person's home or office is covered by the right to privacy under Article 21, and that tapping also touches freedom of speech, so it cannot be done except by a procedure established by law. It did not strike the provision down; instead it laid down binding safeguards until rules were made: only the Union or State Home Secretary may order interception, only where the information cannot reasonably be got another way, orders lapse after a limited period, records must be destroyed when no longer needed, and a review committee must check every order. The petitioners substantially won. This is the reference point for a grievance about unauthorised surveillance or interception of communications by the State.
excerpts: Telephone-Tapping is a serious invasion of an individual's privacy.

telephone conversation in the privacy of one's home or office without interference can certainly be claimed as "right to privacy". Conversations on the telephone are often of an intimate and confidential character.

Holding — the Court held that telephone-tapping is a serious invasion of privacy under Article 21, and laid down procedural safeguards, including authorisation by a senior official and periodic review, that must be followed before telephone interception can be ordered.
bench: Kuldip Singh and S. Saghir Ahmad, JJ.

outcome.winner: PUCL, substantially — the power survived, but under strict safeguards
outcome.verdict: The tapping power was upheld but confined by binding safeguards, including senior-level authorisation, time limits and review committees.

parties.petitioner: People's Union for Civil Liberties
parties.respondent: Union of India

title: People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India
summary: Thousands of workers building stadiums and flyovers in Delhi for the 1982 Asian Games were being paid less than the legal minimum wage, with contractors and middlemen taking a cut, and living in poor conditions on the sites. The People's Union for Democratic Rights wrote to the Supreme Court about what its investigators had found. The Court treated the letter as a petition and held that paying a worker less than the minimum wage fixed under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 amounts to “forced labour”, which Article 23 of the Constitution forbids, because someone driven by poverty to accept less is not working freely. It also held that the Government cannot escape responsibility by pointing at its contractors: it must ensure labour laws are obeyed on its projects, through inspections rather than waiting for complaints. The workers won. This is the reference point for a grievance about construction or contract workers being paid below the legal minimum wage.
excerpts: the complaint in regard to non-payment of minimum wage to the workmen under the Minimum Wages Act 1948, is also one relating to breach of a Fundamental Right enshrined in Article 23 which is violated by non-payment of minimum wage to the workmen.
Article 23 strikes at forced labour in whatever form it may manifest itself, because it is violative of human dignity and is contrary to basic human values.

Holding — the Court held that a worker who is paid less than the minimum wage prescribed by law is a victim of 'forced labour' within the meaning of Article 23, entitling the worker to relief in a writ petition before the Supreme Court.
bench: P.N. Bhagwati and Baharul Islam, JJ.

outcome.winner: The Asiad construction workers
outcome.verdict: Payment below the minimum wage was held to be forced labour barred by Article 23, and the Government was made answerable for its contractors' compliance.

parties.petitioner: People's Union for Democratic Rights
parties.respondent: Union of India, the Delhi Administration and the contractors

statutes.name: Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979

title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
summary: When the Aadhaar biometric identity scheme was challenged in court, the Government argued that Indians have no fundamental right to privacy at all, relying on two old Supreme Court decisions. To settle the question, nine judges of the Supreme Court sat together. They held unanimously that privacy is a fundamental right, protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty and running through the other freedoms in Part III of the Constitution, and overruled the old decisions so far as they had said otherwise. Any intrusion on privacy, by the State or otherwise, must now be backed by law, pursue a legitimate aim, and go no further than necessary. The petitioners won; the validity of Aadhaar itself was decided separately the following year. This is the reference point for grievances about surveillance, data collection, biometric identity and misuse of personal information.
excerpts: The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.
Privacy includes at its core the preservation of personal intimacies, the sanctity of family life, marriage, procreation, the home and sexual orientation.

Holding — the Court held that an invasion of privacy must satisfy the requirements of legality, necessity for a legitimate State aim, and proportionality between the means adopted and the object pursued.
bench: Nine-judge Constitution Bench

outcome.winner: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy and the other petitioners
outcome.verdict: Privacy was declared a fundamental right under Article 21, and intrusions must satisfy legality, necessity and proportionality.

parties.petitioner: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) and other petitioners
parties.respondent: Union of India

statutes.name: Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016

title: R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu
summary: A prisoner on death row in Tamil Nadu, known as Auto Shankar, wrote an account of his life naming police and prison officials he said he had dealt with, and it was to be published in a Tamil magazine. Prison authorities pressed him to disown it and officials warned the magazine not to publish. The magazine's editor, R. Rajagopal, went to the Supreme Court. The Court held that a citizen does have a right to privacy, and that publishing private details of someone's life without consent can be actionable, but that facts already on the public record may be published freely. Crucially, it held that the State and its officials cannot stop a publication in advance: if officials are defamed, their remedy is to sue afterwards, not to gag the press. The magazine won. This is the reference point for a grievance about the State trying to suppress publication or about unauthorised publication of private facts about a person.
excerpts: The right to privacy is implicit in the right to life and liberty guaranteed to the citizens of this country by Article 21. It is a "right to be let alone".
any publication concerning the aforesaid aspects becomes unobjectionable if such publication is based upon public records including court records.

Holding — the Court held that the right to privacy is part of Article 21, but that this right must yield to the freedom of the press where a publication is based on public records, and that state authorities could not restrain publication of the autobiography in advance.
bench: B.P. Jeevan Reddy and S.C. Sen, JJ.

outcome.winner: The magazine and its editor
outcome.verdict: The State was held to have no power of prior restraint, and the magazine was free to publish what appeared from public records.

parties.petitioner: R. Rajagopal, editor of the magazine, and its publisher
parties.respondent: State of Tamil Nadu and its prison and police officials

title: Sahara India Real Estate Corporation Ltd. v. Securities and Exchange Board of India
summary: Two Sahara group companies raised many thousands of crores of rupees from millions of small investors by issuing optionally fully convertible debentures, presenting them as a private placement so that the disclosure, listing and investor-protection rules for public issues would not apply. SEBI investigated and ordered the money refunded with interest. The companies appealed, arguing that SEBI had no business interfering with unlisted companies. The Supreme Court disagreed on every point: an offer made to that many people is a public issue by law, SEBI had jurisdiction to protect those investors, and the companies had broken the law. It dismissed the appeals and ordered the money repaid with interest, with the refund supervised by a retired Supreme Court judge and SEBI free to attach property if the companies did not pay. SEBI and the investors won. This is the reference point for a grievance about a company raising money from the public through securities that evade regulatory disclosure and listing requirements.
excerpts: flouted the mandatory provisions of Section 73(1) of the Companies Act and the consequences provided under Sub-section (2) of Section 73 would, therefore, follow and SEBI had ample powers under Sections 11, 11A and 11B of the SEBI Act to issue directions to refund the amounts to the investors with interest.

Saharas having failed to make application for listing on any of the recognized stock exchange, as provided under Section 73(1) of the Companies Act, become legally liable to refund the amount collected from the subscribers in pursuance to their RHPs, along with interest as provided under Section 73(2) of the Act.

Holding — the Court upheld SEBI's finding that the Sahara companies had raised funds from the public without complying with securities disclosure and listing requirements, and directed refund of the amounts collected to investors with interest.
bench: K.S. Radhakrishnan and Jagdish Singh Khehar, JJ.

outcome.winner: SEBI and the investors
outcome.verdict: The appeals were dismissed and the Sahara companies were ordered to refund investors' money with interest, under the supervision of a retired Supreme Court judge.

parties.petitioner: Sahara India Real Estate Corporation Ltd. and Sahara Housing Investment Corporation Ltd. (appealing)
parties.respondent: Securities and Exchange Board of India

statutes.name: Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992

title: Chintalapati Srinivasa Raju v. Securities and Exchange Board of India (Satyam)
citation: Civil Appeal No. 16805 of 2017 (Supreme Court, 14 May 2018)
summary: In January 2009 the chairman of Satyam Computer Services confessed that the company's published accounts had been inflated for years, in what became India's largest corporate accounting fraud. The securities regulator, SEBI, then acted against his relatives and family companies as well, barring them from the securities market and stripping gains from their sales of Satyam shares. They appealed to the Supreme Court. The Court held that SEBI must prove each person's own involvement and cannot go beyond the case set out in its show-cause notice, and it set aside the orders against most of the relatives, including a former director who was found not to be a promoter of the company. It upheld the orders against the promoters' holding company and against the relative who had actually arranged share sales at manipulated prices for the promoters. The result was mixed: the regulator's orders stood only against those whose involvement was actually shown. This is the reference point for grievances about accounting fraud, falsified financial statements and losses suffered by shareholders and employees.
excerpts: Once it is demonstrated that he is not a promoter, the findings of the Whole Time Member and the majority view of the Appellate Tribunal must be set aside as they go beyond the show cause notice.

Holding — the Court held that a person cannot be found liable on a case that was never put to him in the show-cause notice, and set aside the orders against the appellants whose involvement in the fraud had not been established.

Holding — the orders against the promoters' holding company and against the relative who arranged sales of shares at manipulated prices for the promoters were upheld, and those appeals were dismissed.
bench: R.F. Nariman and Navin Sinha, JJ.

outcome.winner: Mixed — most appellants were cleared, two were not
outcome.verdict: SEBI's orders were set aside against most of the appellants for going beyond the show-cause notice, but upheld against the promoters' holding company and the relative who arranged the share sales.

parties.petitioner: Chintalapati Srinivasa Raju and other relatives and companies of the Satyam promoters
parties.respondent: Securities and Exchange Board of India

statutes.name: Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992

title: Shantistar Builders v. Narayan Khimalal Totame
summary: A builder in Maharashtra was allowed to keep surplus urban land under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 on condition that it build low-cost housing for the weaker sections of society. People entitled to that housing complained that the scheme was not reaching them and that the builder had been permitted to raise its rates, and the Bombay High Court ordered that the scheme be monitored. Shantistar Builders appealed against that monitoring to the Supreme Court. The Court refused to lift it. It held that the right to life includes the right to a decent, livable home rather than mere shelter, and that schemes meant for the poor must be protected from being defeated in practice: it directed that committees headed by a judicial officer scrutinise applicants and supervise such schemes across Maharashtra, and told the State to amend its code accordingly. The builder lost, and the intended beneficiaries won stronger supervision. This is the reference point for a grievance about a developer failing to deliver adequate housing promised under a low-income housing scheme.
excerpts: Basic needs of man have traditionally been accepted to be three-food, clothing and shelter. The right to life is guaranteed in any civilized society. That would take within its sweep the right to food, the right to clothing, the right to decent environment and a reasonable accommodation to live in.

The difference between the need of an animal and a human being for shelter has to be kept in view. For the animal it is the bare protection of the body; for a human being it has to be a suitable accommodation which would allow him to grow in every aspect - physical, mental and intellectual.

Holding — the Court held that the right to life under Article 21 includes the right to shelter for the poor, meaning a habitable and livable accommodation that allows a person to grow physically, mentally and intellectually, and not a bare roof over one's head.
bench: Ranganath Misra, P.B. Sawant and K. Ramaswamy, JJ.

outcome.winner: The weaker-section applicants the scheme was meant for
outcome.verdict: The builder's challenge failed and the Court ordered judicially headed committees to vet applicants and supervise such housing schemes.

parties.petitioner: Shantistar Builders (appealing)
parties.respondent: Narayan Khimalal Totame and other low-income applicants

title: Spring Meadows Hospital v. Harjot Ahluwalia
summary: A young boy was admitted to Spring Meadows Hospital in Delhi with typhoid. A nurse gave him an injection intravenously; he went into cardiac arrest within moments and suffered brain damage that left him in a permanent vegetative state. His parents complained under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, and the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission awarded compensation to the child for his care and, separately, to the parents for their mental agony. The hospital appealed, arguing that the parents were not its consumers and that it had since treated the child free of charge. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals with costs: parents who engage a hospital for their child are consumers too, and a hospital is liable for the negligence of the staff it employs. The family won. This is the reference point for a grievance about medical negligence and deficiency of service by a hospital or clinic.
excerpts: It is a great mistake to think that doctors and hospitals are easy targets for the dissatisfied patient.

When a young child is taken to a hospital by his parents and the child is treated by the doctor, the parents would come within the definition of consumer having hired the services and the young child would also become a consumer under the inclusive definition being a beneficiary of such services.

Holding — the Court held that both the parents, who had hired the hospital's services, and the minor child, as beneficiary of those services, were separately 'consumers' under Section 2(1)(d) of the Consumer Protection Act and could each recover compensation for the injury each had sustained.
bench: S. Saghir Ahmad and G.B. Pattanaik, JJ.

outcome.winner: The child and his parents
outcome.verdict: The hospital's appeals were dismissed with costs, and compensation to both the child and his parents was upheld.

parties.petitioner: Spring Meadows Hospital and its staff (appealing)
parties.respondent: Harjol Ahluwalia, the child patient, through his parents

title: Vedanta Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu (Sterlite copper smelter, Thoothukudi)
summary: Vedanta's Sterlite copper smelter at Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu was shut down in 2018 by the State Government and the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board, after years of complaints from people living nearby and repeated breaches of pollution norms. Vedanta challenged the closure, lost in the Madras High Court, and appealed to the Supreme Court. The Court refused to interfere, holding that the number, repetition and seriousness of the violations left the authorities and the High Court no other honest option, and that the health and welfare of the residents outweighed the plant's contribution to the economy. The company lost and the plant stays closed; the State's regulator was also told its own slowness in enforcing the law had been rightly criticised. This is the reference point for a grievance about a factory or industrial plant harming the air, water or health of a nearby community.
excerpts: While the industry has played a role in economic growth, the health and welfare of the residents of the area is a matter of utmost concern.

The nature of the violations and the repeated nature of the breaches coupled with the severity of the breach of environmental norms would in the ultimate analysis have left neither the statutory authorities nor the High Court with the option to take any other view unless they were to be oblivious of their plain duty.

Holding — the Supreme Court declined to interfere with the closure of the copper smelter, dismissing Vedanta's petitions and leaving the orders of the State Government and the Pollution Control Board in force.
bench: Dr D.Y. Chandrachud C.J.I., J.B. Pardiwala and Manoj Misra, JJ.

outcome.winner: The State of Tamil Nadu and the residents of Thoothukudi
outcome.verdict: Vedanta's petitions were dismissed and the 2018 closure of the copper smelter was upheld.

parties.petitioner: Vedanta Ltd., the operator of the Sterlite copper smelter
parties.respondent: State of Tamil Nadu and the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board

statutes.name: Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974

title: Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar
summary: Subhash Kumar petitioned the Supreme Court claiming that West Bokaro Collieries and Tata Iron and Steel Company were discharging slurry from their washeries into the Bokaro river in Bihar, polluting water the people downstream depended on. The Court used the case to state a principle that has been relied on ever since: the right to life under Article 21 includes the right to enjoy pollution-free water and air, and any citizen may come directly to the Supreme Court to protect it. On the facts, however, it found no material to support the allegation, and found that the petitioner himself had been buying slurry from the company for years and had brought the case because it refused to sell him more. Holding that a public interest petition cannot be used for a private grudge, the Court dismissed the petition and ordered the petitioner to pay costs to the companies. The petitioner lost. This is the reference point for a grievance about a company polluting a river or water source that a community depends on.
excerpts: Right to life is a fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution and it includes the right of enjoyment of pollution free water and air for full enjoyment of life.

If anything endangers or impairs that quality of life in derogation of laws, a citizen has right to have recourse to Article 32 of the Constitution for removing the pollution of water or air which may be detrimental to the quality of life.

Holding — the Court held that the right to a pollution-free environment is part of the right to life under Article 21, and that a citizen may invoke the writ jurisdiction under Article 32 to seek relief against pollution of a river or water source.
bench: K.N. Singh and N.D. Ojha, JJ.

outcome.winner: The State and the companies
outcome.verdict: The right to pollution-free water was recognised, but the petition was dismissed as a private grievance dressed up as public interest, with costs against the petitioner.

parties.petitioner: Subhash Kumar
parties.respondent: State of Bihar, West Bokaro Collieries and Tata Iron and Steel Company

statutes.name: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974

title: Sudama Singh v. Government of Delhi
summary: Delhi's agencies demolished jhuggi clusters to make way for road and drain works, and refused to resettle the families living there, taking the position that people whose homes stood on a road's “right of way” were not entitled to relocation at all. Sudama Singh and other residents challenged that refusal in the Delhi High Court. The Court held the position illegal and unconstitutional: the residents were entitled to be considered under the city's relocation policy, and before any eviction the State must survey the families, consult them meaningfully, and relocate those who qualify to a site with basic civic amenities. It directed that eligible petitioners be granted alternative sites within four months, and that the judgment be publicised among jhuggi residents across the city. The residents won. This is the reference point for a grievance about a slum demolition or eviction carried out without a proper survey or resettlement plan.
excerpts: The government will be failing in its statutory and constitutional obligation if it fails to identify spaces equipped infrastructurally with the civic amenities that can ensure a decent living to those being relocated prior to initiating the moves for eviction.
Each of the above factors will have to be borne in mind before any task for forceful eviction of a jhuggi cluster is undertaken by the State agencies.

Holding — the Court held that before undertaking eviction and demolition of a slum settlement, the authorities must conduct a meaningful survey of the residents and consider their entitlement to rehabilitation, so that relocation does not leave them worse off.
bench: Chief Justice and S. Muralidhar, J.

outcome.winner: The jhuggi residents
outcome.verdict: The refusal to relocate “right of way” dwellers was struck down, and eligible residents were ordered to be given alternative sites with civic amenities within four months.

parties.petitioner: Sudama Singh and other jhuggi dwellers
parties.respondent: Government of Delhi and its civic agencies

title: Swaraj Abhiyan v. Union of India
summary: Large parts of India were hit by drought in 2015 and 2016, and the citizens' group Swaraj Abhiyan went to the Supreme Court because Union and State Governments were not delivering the relief that the law already promised. This judgment deals with food and work. The Court directed that a household in a drought-hit area must not be denied its food-grain entitlement under the National Food Security Act, 2013 merely because it has no ration card, that mid-day meals must be provided to schoolchildren through the summer vacation in those areas, and that workers under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 must be paid on time, with compensation when payment is delayed. It criticised governments for leaving parts of these laws a dead letter, and kept the case open to watch compliance. The petitioners won. This is the reference point for a grievance about a State Government failing to deliver statutory food security or drought relief entitlements.
excerpts: at least 1/4th of the country's population (if not 1/3rd) is affected by drought and the State Governments must take appropriate steps to ensure that at least the statutory requirement of food grains is made available to the people in the drought affected areas of the country.
there is nothing to suggest that without edible oils and dal/lentil the fundamental right of the people in drought affected areas guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution is violated.

Holding — the Court directed State Governments to ensure the statutory foodgrain entitlement under the National Food Security Act reached households in drought-affected areas, and to consider with compassion any request for additional relief such as dal, edible oil or an extended Mid-Day Meal Scheme.
bench: Madan B. Lokur and N.V. Ramana, JJ.

outcome.winner: Swaraj Abhiyan and the drought-affected households
outcome.verdict: Directions were issued on food-grain entitlements, mid-day meals and timely wage payment, and the case was kept open to monitor compliance.

parties.petitioner: Swaraj Abhiyan, a citizens' group
parties.respondent: Union of India and the drought-affected State Governments

statutes.name: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005

title: Union Carbide Corporation v. Union of India
summary: In December 1984, methyl isocyanate gas leaked from the Union Carbide pesticide plant in Bhopal and killed or maimed people in their thousands, in the worst industrial disaster in India's history. In 1989 the Supreme Court approved a settlement in which the company paid 470 million US dollars, and all civil claims and the criminal prosecutions were brought to an end. Victims' organisations and others asked the Court to review that settlement. In this judgment the Court upheld the settlement amount and its power to have approved it, but held that stopping the criminal cases had not been justified: it revived the prosecution of those accused, and held that if the settlement fund turned out to be too small to pay the victims, the Union of India must make up the shortfall. The outcome was mixed — the company kept the financial settlement, while the victims regained the criminal case and a government guarantee against a shortfall. This is the reference point for a grievance about a corporation's mass-harm liability being resolved through an inadequate settlement that displaces individual accountability.
excerpts: The Union Carbide Corporation shall pay a sum of U.S. Dollars 470 millions (Four hundred and seventy Millions) to the Union of India in full settlement of all claims, rights and liabilities related to and arising out of the Bhopal Gas disaster.

The Court had no power to withdraw to itself those criminal proceedings and quash them. The orders of the Court dated 14th and 15th of February 1989, in so far as they pertain to the quashing of criminal proceedings are without jurisdiction.

Holding — the Court upheld the civil settlement of 470 million US dollars paid by Union Carbide for the Bhopal gas disaster, but held that the Court had exceeded its jurisdiction in quashing the pending criminal prosecution as part of that settlement, and revived the criminal proceedings.
bench: Rangnath Misra, K.N. Singh and A.M. Ahmadi, JJ.

outcome.winner: Mixed — the settlement stood, the criminal prosecution was restored
outcome.verdict: The 1989 settlement was upheld, but the quashing of the criminal proceedings was set aside and the Union of India was made liable for any shortfall in the fund.

parties.petitioner: Bhopal gas victims' organisations and others challenging the settlement
parties.respondent: Union Carbide Corporation and the Union of India

statutes.name: Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985

title: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India
summary: Tanneries in Tamil Nadu were pouring untreated effluent into the Palar river and on to surrounding farmland, spoiling the main source of drinking water for the people of the area. The Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum took the case to the Supreme Court. The Court held that sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle are part of Indian law: an industry must prevent harm it cannot be sure about, and must pay both to compensate victims and to restore the damaged environment. It ordered the Central Government to set up an authority under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 to assess the loss and fix compensation, imposed a pollution fine on every tannery in the affected districts, required each one to install effluent treatment or be closed, and handed continuing supervision to a special “Green Bench” of the Madras High Court. The residents won. This is the reference point for a grievance about untreated industrial effluent damaging a river, farmland or drinking water source.
excerpts: Remediation of the damaged environment is part of the process of "Sustainable Development" and as such polluter is liable to pay the cost to the individual sufferers as well as the cost of reversing the damaged ecology.

The precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle have been accepted as part of the law of the land. Article 21 of the Constitution of India guarantees protection of life and personal liberty.

Holding — the Court held that the precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle are part of Indian environmental law, and directed the tanneries to close or install effluent treatment and to pay for restoring the ecology of the affected area.
bench: Kuldip Singh and K. Venkataswami, JJ.

outcome.winner: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum and the affected residents
outcome.verdict: An authority was ordered to assess and recover compensation, fines were imposed on the tanneries, and effluent treatment was made a condition of staying open.

parties.petitioner: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum
parties.respondent: Union of India, the State of Tamil Nadu and the tanneries

statutes.name: Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974

title: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
summary: A social worker in Rajasthan was gang-raped in revenge for trying to stop a child marriage, and it became clear that India had no law at all against sexual harassment at work. Women's rights groups, led by Vishaka, petitioned the Supreme Court. The Court held that sexual harassment at the workplace violates a woman's rights to equality, to work and to live with dignity, and that employers are responsible for preventing it. Because Parliament had not legislated, it laid down guidelines that every employer had to follow, including a complaints committee headed by a woman, and made them binding and enforceable law until Parliament acted. The petitioners won, and those guidelines governed Indian workplaces until the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 was passed. This is the reference point for a workplace harassment or workplace safety grievance.
excerpts: Each such incident results in violation of the fundamental rights of 'Gender Equality' and the 'Right of Life and Liberty'.
It is necessary and expedient for employers in work places as well as other responsible persons or institutions to observe certain guidelines to ensure the prevention of sexual harassment of women:
Holding — the Court held that the guidelines it laid down would be binding and enforceable under Article 32 until suitable legislation was enacted to occupy the field.
bench: J.S. Verma C.J., Sujata V. Manohar, B.N. Kirpal, JJ.

outcome.winner: Vishaka and the women's groups
outcome.verdict: Binding workplace guidelines against sexual harassment were laid down, enforceable until Parliament legislated.

parties.petitioner: Vishaka and other women's rights groups
parties.respondent: State of Rajasthan and the Union of India

statutes.name: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013

title: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha & Ors.
summary: Doctors and hospitals, through the Indian Medical Association, argued that patients should not be able to take medical negligence complaints to the consumer courts, on the ground that treatment is not a “service” under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. The question reached the Supreme Court after courts and consumer commissions across the country had answered it differently. The Court held that medical treatment is a service under the Act, so a patient who pays a doctor or hospital, or whose treatment is paid for by an employer or insurer, can bring a negligence complaint in the consumer forum, which is faster and cheaper than a civil suit. Only a hospital that treats every patient entirely free of charge falls outside the Act. The doctors' association lost, and patients gained a practical way to hold doctors and hospitals to account. This is the reference point for a grievance about being unable to hold a doctor or hospital accountable for substandard treatment.
excerpts: Medical practitioners do not enjoy any immunity and they can be sued in contract or tort on the ground that they have failed to exercise reasonable skill and care.

Keeping in view the wide amplitude of the definition of `service' in the main part of Section 2(1)(o) as construed by this Court in Lucknow Development Authority (supra), we find no plausible reason to cut down the width of that part so as to exclude the services rendered by a medical practitioner from the ambit of the main part of Section 2(1)(o).

Holding — the Court held that service rendered by a medical practitioner or hospital for a fee, including where some patients are treated free of charge and cross-subsidised by paying patients, falls within the definition of 'service' under the Consumer Protection Act, making such patients 'consumers' entitled to complain of deficiency in service.
bench: S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria, JJ.

outcome.winner: Patients
outcome.verdict: Medical services were held to be a “service” under the Consumer Protection Act, so negligence complaints can be brought in the consumer forums.

parties.petitioner: Indian Medical Association, for doctors and hospitals
parties.respondent: V.P. Shantha and other patients who had complained to consumer forums
